title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
hook: a mother checks her toddler's mouth for dirt and sees the whole universe inside
carry: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: the wheel of offering. Food from rain, rain from offering, offering from action, and whoever takes without giving back is a thief. Today, the bhakti road again. Day three hundred six.

Every parent of a toddler knows this moment. Another kid runs up and announces: he ate dirt! And you crouch down, and you say the words: open your mouth. In the village of Gokul, the other boys run to Yashoda: Krishna ate dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, all innocence, and says: I didn't. They're lying. If you don't believe me, look for yourself. And he opens his mouth. What Yashoda sees in there is one of the most famous scenes in all of Hindu storytelling.
screen: `HE ATE DIRT!` → `I DIDN'T. LOOK FOR YOURSELF.` → `HE OPENS HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Inside her son's mouth, the Bhagavata Purana says, Yashoda sees everything. The sky and all its directions. The stars and planets. Mountains, islands, oceans. Wind and fire and the moon. And then, somewhere in all that, she sees the village of Gokul, and in it, herself, standing there looking into her son's mouth. You can imagine what happens to her. She's shaken to the core. Is this a dream? she wonders. A trick? Or is this child something beyond anything I can understand? She begins, the text says, to take refuge in the one whose nature is beyond thought. And then the story does something tender. Krishna, the text says, spreads his power of affection over her, the covering the tradition calls maya, and she forgets. The vision fades. She takes him back on her lap, and she's just his mother again, and he's just her little boy, and she loves him more than ever. Think about what that means for the bhakti road. The vision was real. But Krishna didn't want Yashoda to relate to him as the cosmic Lord, trembling in awe. He wanted to be held and scolded and fed. Many devotees say this is the heart of it: God enjoys being loved as a child, a friend, a beloved, more than being feared as a king. The universe fits in his mouth. And he'd rather sit in your lap.
screen: `THE UNIVERSE IN HIS MOUTH.` · `YASHODA SEES HERSELF THERE.` · `THEN SHE FORGETS.` · `HE'D RATHER BE HELD THAN FEARED.` · then, large: `THE UNIVERSE FITS IN HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of something enormous: the night sky, the ocean, the number of people alive right now. Let it be too big to hold. Breathe in, and feel the awe of it. Then breathe out, and bring it close, the way Yashoda held her child. Something very small and near: your own hands, a cup of tea, someone's face you love. Let the enormous and the near sit together. If you pray, you can speak to God as someone close, not only someone vast. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and today the action is a mother's: crouching down, looking in, and loving him anyway.

Your line names the three roads: karma, the Gita's third chapter; bhakti, the Bhagavata's Krishna stories; jnana, the Upanishads. Today, look closely at one ordinary face, and remember whole worlds might be in there. Day three hundred six.

howItsDone: Devotees of Krishna retell the stories of his childhood in Gokul and Vrindavan in songs, dance and festival plays, especially at Janmashtami, and many relate to him with vatsalya, the tender love of a parent for a child.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the entire universe inside your toddler's mouth. what happens next in the story?
options: you bow down and never treat him as your child again.
you run and tell the whole village.
the vision fades, you forget, and you hold him in your lap.
fork.reveal: Krishna covers her with affection and she forgets. devotees say he'd rather be loved as a child than feared as a king.

original.note: Sanskrit: tender love, as of a parent for a child (from vatsa, a calf). One of the moods of bhakti.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story to prove Krishna is God.
what it means: the vision is real, but Krishna chooses to be loved as a child, not feared as a Lord.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata 10.8: Krishna's yogamaya veils the vision so Yashoda's vatsalya can continue; later Vaishnava theology ranks intimate love of this kind very high.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.8.32–10.8.45 (the universe in Krishna's mouth)
